candidateEvidence.excerpt: An Ohio man was sentenced on September 8 to 15 years in prison in a case involving threats, cyberstalking and real and AI-generated sexual images of women and children. The U.S. Attorney’s Office says James Strahler II’s conviction for publishing digital forgeries was the first under the Take It Down Act.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: The DOJ page is dated September 8, 2026 and reports that James Strahler II was sentenced to 180 months for cybercrimes involving real and AI-generated sexually explicit images and threats. The page lists guilty pleas to cyberstalking, producing obscene visual representations of child sexual abuse, and publication of digital forgeries. It describes that conviction as part of the Take It Down Act, enacted in 2025. The DOJ calls the prosecution the first in the nation under the Act and describes harassment and images involving adult women and children.
A prosecution press release is not a sentencing transcript and gives no count-by-count allocation. The first-conviction claim remains attributed to the U.S. Attorney’s Office.

The FTC says image-based abuse includes real, digitally altered, and AI-generated intimate images shared without consent. The FTC says certain platforms must provide a removal request process and remove the image and known identical copies within 48 hours. The FTC routes platform failures to TakeItDown.ftc.gov and reports about perpetrators to local law enforcement or the FBI.
U.S. framework; platform coverage and valid-request conditions apply. It does not promise worldwide erasure.

candidateEvidence.excerpt: There are two separate jobs here: holding the perpetrator accountable and getting the image taken down. A criminal sentence addresses the first. The platform hosting the image has a different role in the second. A prison sentence does not automatically erase copies from the internet.

A fake image can cause real abuse. This case has reached sentencing, but punishing the perpetrator and getting an image removed are separate processes. The U.S. Take It Down Act also gives people a route to request removal from covered platforms.
